[1] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 5 | Section: 4.1 Open-domain Question Answering
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
It is worth noting that RAG’s retriever is initialized using DPR’s retriever, which uses retrieval supervision on Natural Questions and TriviaQA. RAG compares favourably to the DPR QA system, which uses a BERT-based “cross- encoder” to re-rank documents, along with an extractive reader. RAG demonstrates that neither a re-ranker nor extractive reader is necessary for state-of-the-art performance. There are several advantages to generating answers even when it is possible to extract them.

[2] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 4 | Section: 3.2 Abstractive Question Answering
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
3.2 Abstractive Question Answering RAG models can go beyond simple extractive QA and answer questions with free-form, abstractive text generation. To test RAG’s natural language generation (NLG) in a knowledge-intensive setting, we use the MSMARCO NLG task v2.1 [43].

[3] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 6 | Section: 4.2 Abstractive Question Answering
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
4.2 Abstractive Question Answering As shown in Table 2, RAG-Sequence outperforms BART on Open MS-MARCO NLG by 2.6 Bleu points and 2.6 Rouge-L points. RAG approaches state-of-the-art model performance, which is impressive given that (i) those models access gold passages with speciﬁc information required to generate the reference answer , (ii) many questions are unanswerable without the gold passages, and (iii) not all questions are answerable from Wikipedia alone.

[4] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 4 | Section: 3.1 Open-domain Question Answering
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
3.1 Open-domain Question Answering Open-domain question answering (QA) is an important real-world application and common testbed for knowledge-intensive tasks [20]. We treat questions and answers as input-output text pairs (x, y) and train RAG by directly minimizing the negative log-likelihood of answers. We compare RAG to the popular extractive QA paradigm [5, 7, 31, 26], where answers are extracted spans from retrieved documents, relying primarily on non-parametric knowledge.

[5] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 2 | Section: 1 Introduction
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
Our results highlight the beneﬁts of combining parametric and non-parametric memory with genera- tion for knowledge-intensive tasks—tasks that humans could not reasonably be expected to perform without access to an external knowledge source. Our RAG models achieve state-of-the-art results on open Natural Questions [29], WebQuestions [3] and CuratedTrec [2] and strongly outperform recent approaches that use specialised pre-training objectives on TriviaQA [24].

[6] Source: 2004.04906v3.pdf | Page: 7 | Section: 6.1 End-to-end QA System
Title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
6.1 End-to-end QA System We implement an end-to-end question answering system in which we can plug different retriever systems directly. Besides the retriever, our QA sys- tem consists of a neural reader that outputs the answer to the question. Given the top k retrieved passages (up to 100 in our experiments), the reader assigns a passage selection score to each passage. In addition, it extracts an answer span from each passage and assigns a span score.

[7] Source: 2004.04906v3.pdf | Page: 12 | Section: 8 Conclusion
Title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
A Distant Supervision When training our ﬁnal DPR model using Natural Questions, we use the passages in our collection that best match the gold context as the positive passages. As some QA datasets contain only the question and answer pairs, it is thus interesting to see when using the passages that contain the answers as positives (i.e., the distant supervision setting), whether there is a signiﬁcant performance degradation.

[8] Source: 2004.04906v3.pdf | Page: 8 | Section: 6.2 Results
Title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
While both methods include addi- tional pretraining tasks and employ an expensive end-to-end training regime, DPR manages to out- perform them on both NQ and TriviaQA, simply by focusing on learning a strong passage retrieval model using pairs of questions and answers. The additional pretraining tasks are likely more useful only when the target training sets are small.

[9] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 3 | Section: 2.2 Retriever: DPR
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
2.2 Retriever: DPR The retrieval component pη(z|x) is based on DPR [26]. DPR follows a bi-encoder architecture: pη(z|x) ∝exp � d(z)⊤q(x)  d(z) = BERTd(z), q(x) = BERTq(x) where d(z) is a dense representation of a document produced by a BERTBASE document encoder [8], and q(x) a query representation produced by a query encoder, also based on BERTBASE.

Title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering

根据所提供证据，DPR 端到端 QA 系统的答案选择机制如下：在给定检索到的前 k 个段落（实验中最多 100 个）后，reader 会为每个段落分配一个段落选择分数，并从每个段落中抽取答案片段并分配片段分数[6]。因此，其输出受限于从检索段落中抽取的答案片段这一约束。

RAG 的抽象式 QA 能力则不同：RAG 模型可以超越简单的抽取式 QA，以自由形式的抽象式文本生成来回答问题[2]。也就是说，RAG 的输出不局限于抽取片段，而可以是生成的自由文本。

关于两者“输出约束差异”的直接对比，现有证据只能分别支持上述两点（DPR reader 抽取答案片段[6]；RAG 可进行抽象式生成[2]），并未直接给出两者约束差异的显式比较陈述。

Besides the retriever, our QA sys- tem consists of a neural reader that outputs the answer to the question. Given the top k retrieved passages (up to 100 in our experiments), the reader assigns a passage selection score to each passage. In addition, it extracts an answer span from each passage and assigns a span score.

api_calls.prompt:
You are a query decomposition assistant for a scientific paper RAG system.

Your task is to analyze the user's question and determine
whether it requires multiple independent information searches.

Rules:
1. Do not answer the question.
2. If the question has only one information need,
   do not decompose it.
3. If the question requires multiple distinct pieces of evidence,
   generate between 2 and 4 sub-questions.

4. The sub-questions must be a decomposition of the original question.
   Do NOT include the original question itself as a sub-question.

5. Each sub-question should answer only one distinct information need
   required to answer the original question.
   For comparisons with multiple entities AND multiple requested aspects,
   split by entity and by aspect when the total fits within 4.
   For example, comparing Method A and Method B on representation and scoring
   requires four searches: A representation, A scoring, B representation,
   and B scoring. Do not combine representation and scoring in one search.
   For vector-retrieval questions, keep concrete retrieval vocabulary:
   representation searches should explicitly ask about query/document vectors
   or embeddings; scoring searches should ask how similarity between them is
   computed. Do not assume or name a particular scoring function in the query.

6. Preserve the exact entities, model names, paper names,
   abbreviations, and technical terms from the original question.

7. If the original question compares multiple specific models,
   methods, or papers, create separate sub-questions for each
   specific entity being compared.

8. Each sub-question must explicitly mention the relevant entity.
   Do not replace a specific entity with a generic term.

9. Preserve the factual intent of the original question.
   Do not introduce words such as "typical", "common", "usually",
   or "in general" unless they appear in the original question.

10. Do not make the sub-question broader or more general than
    the original question.

11. Return only valid JSON, without explanations or markdown.

Example:

Original question:
How do VGG and DCNN differ in their use of convolutional filter sizes?

Correct decomposition:
{
    "needs_decomposition": true,
    "sub_queries": [
        "According to the VGG paper, what convolutional filter sizes are used?",
        "According to the DCNN paper, what convolutional filter sizes are used?"
    ]
}

Incorrect decomposition:
{
    "needs_decomposition": true,
    "sub_queries": [
        "How do VGG and DCNN differ in their use of convolutional filter sizes?",
        "What are the typical convolutional filter sizes used in VGG networks?",
        "What are the typical convolutional filter sizes used in DCNN networks?"
    ]
}

Output format:
{
    "needs_decomposition": boolean,
    "sub_queries": ["question 1", "question 2"]
}

If decomposition is unnecessary, return an empty sub_queries list.

Original Question:
How does the DPR end-to-end QA system select its final answer, and how does its output constraint differ from the abstractive QA capability described in RAG?

You are an AI research assistant.

Answer the user's question based only on the provided context.

Rules:
1. Do not invent information or introduce unsupported claims.
2. Place citations immediately after the claims they support.
3. Cite only context chunks that directly support each claim.
4. Every citation must directly support the exact claim it follows. Mentioning the same topic is not sufficient evidence.
5. Do not combine separate statements into a causal relationship unless the source explicitly establishes that relationship.
6. Do not attribute technical claims to a paper unless the context directly supports those claims.
7. If a claim cannot be directly supported, omit it or clearly state that the evidence is insufficient.
8. Keep the answer focused on the question.

9. A source filename identifies the document, not necessarily the model described in a passage. Check named subjects and the cited surrounding text.
10. Evidence guidance supplements the original passages. Subject hints are rule-based; check them against the sources. For kernel H x W x C, H x W is the spatial size and C is channels per kernel; a kernel count is not a spatial size. Preserve layer numbers and configuration qualifiers.

11. Respond in Simplified Chinese unless the question explicitly requests another language. Keep technical names in their original form.
12. For unsupported parts of the question, state the missing evidence concisely. Do not substitute measurements from other hardware, datasets or settings, or append unrelated facts to a refusal. For an entirely unsupported Chinese question, begin with 当前证据不足 and explain what is missing in only one or two sentences, without any supplementary measurements.
13. Answer only the scope actually requested. Missing unasked details are not grounds for an insufficiency warning. When the requested main facts are supported, answer them directly.

[1] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 5 | Section: 4.1 Open-domain Question Answering
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
It is worth noting that RAG’s retriever is initialized using DPR’s retriever, which uses retrieval supervision on Natural Questions and TriviaQA. RAG compares favourably to the DPR QA system, which uses a BERT-based “cross- encoder” to re-rank documents, along with an extractive reader. RAG demonstrates that neither a re-ranker nor extractive reader is necessary for state-of-the-art performance. There are several advantages to generating answers even when it is possible to extract them.

[2] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 4 | Section: 3.2 Abstractive Question Answering
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
3.2 Abstractive Question Answering RAG models can go beyond simple extractive QA and answer questions with free-form, abstractive text generation. To test RAG’s natural language generation (NLG) in a knowledge-intensive setting, we use the MSMARCO NLG task v2.1 [43].

[3] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 6 | Section: 4.2 Abstractive Question Answering
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
4.2 Abstractive Question Answering As shown in Table 2, RAG-Sequence outperforms BART on Open MS-MARCO NLG by 2.6 Bleu points and 2.6 Rouge-L points. RAG approaches state-of-the-art model performance, which is impressive given that (i) those models access gold passages with speciﬁc information required to generate the reference answer , (ii) many questions are unanswerable without the gold passages, and (iii) not all questions are answerable from Wikipedia alone.

[4] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 4 | Section: 3.1 Open-domain Question Answering
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
3.1 Open-domain Question Answering Open-domain question answering (QA) is an important real-world application and common testbed for knowledge-intensive tasks [20]. We treat questions and answers as input-output text pairs (x, y) and train RAG by directly minimizing the negative log-likelihood of answers. We compare RAG to the popular extractive QA paradigm [5, 7, 31, 26], where answers are extracted spans from retrieved documents, relying primarily on non-parametric knowledge.

[5] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 2 | Section: 1 Introduction
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
Our results highlight the beneﬁts of combining parametric and non-parametric memory with genera- tion for knowledge-intensive tasks—tasks that humans could not reasonably be expected to perform without access to an external knowledge source. Our RAG models achieve state-of-the-art results on open Natural Questions [29], WebQuestions [3] and CuratedTrec [2] and strongly outperform recent approaches that use specialised pre-training objectives on TriviaQA [24].

6.1 End-to-end QA System We implement an end-to-end question answering system in which we can plug different retriever systems directly. Besides the retriever, our QA sys- tem consists of a neural reader that outputs the answer to the question. Given the top k retrieved passages (up to 100 in our experiments), the reader assigns a passage selection score to each passage. In addition, it extracts an answer span from each passage and assigns a span score.

[7] Source: 2004.04906v3.pdf | Page: 12 | Section: 8 Conclusion
Title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
A Distant Supervision When training our ﬁnal DPR model using Natural Questions, we use the passages in our collection that best match the gold context as the positive passages. As some QA datasets contain only the question and answer pairs, it is thus interesting to see when using the passages that contain the answers as positives (i.e., the distant supervision setting), whether there is a signiﬁcant performance degradation.

[8] Source: 2004.04906v3.pdf | Page: 8 | Section: 6.2 Results
Title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
While both methods include addi- tional pretraining tasks and employ an expensive end-to-end training regime, DPR manages to out- perform them on both NQ and TriviaQA, simply by focusing on learning a strong passage retrieval model using pairs of questions and answers. The additional pretraining tasks are likely more useful only when the target training sets are small.

[9] Source: 2005.11401v4.pdf | Page: 3 | Section: 2.2 Retriever: DPR
Title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
2.2 Retriever: DPR The retrieval component pη(z|x) is based on DPR [26]. DPR follows a bi-encoder architecture: pη(z|x) ∝exp � d(z)⊤q(x)  d(z) = BERTd(z), q(x) = BERTq(x) where d(z) is a dense representation of a document produced by a BERTBASE document encoder [8], and q(x) a query representation produced by a query encoder, also based on BERTBASE.

Title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
When evaluated on a wide range of open-domain QA datasets, our dense retriever outperforms a strong Lucene- BM25 system greatly by 9%-19% absolute in terms of top-20 passage retrieval accuracy, and helps our end-to-end QA system establish new state-of-the-art on multiple open-domain QA benchmarks.1

Question:
How does the DPR end-to-end QA system select its final answer, and how does its output constraint differ from the abstractive QA capability described in RAG?

Before writing the final answer:
- Synthesize the passages. Where a configuration exception is stated, describe the main pattern as mainly or predominantly and include the exception in the same sentence. Do not repeat an all/only statement that conflicts with that exception. An exception must change the same property; keep independent design choices separate.
- For why questions, explain each supported mechanism. When comparing alternatives, explicitly state their supported equivalent property and quantities, rather than leaving the equivalence implicit in the phrase instead of.
- Omit unnecessary background and names absent from the passages. Do not repeat the same point or list unasked ablations and implementation details.

response.answer:
根据所提供证据，DPR 端到端 QA 系统的答案选择机制如下：在给定检索到的前 k 个段落（实验中最多 100 个）后，reader 会为每个段落分配一个段落选择分数，并从每个段落中抽取答案片段并分配片段分数[6]。因此，其输出受限于从检索段落中抽取的答案片段这一约束。

RAG 的抽象式 QA 能力则不同：RAG 模型可以超越简单的抽取式 QA，以自由形式的抽象式文本生成来回答问题[2]。也就是说，RAG 的输出不局限于抽取片段，而可以是生成的自由文本。

关于两者“输出约束差异”的直接对比，现有证据只能分别支持上述两点（DPR reader 抽取答案片段[6]；RAG 可进行抽象式生成[2]），并未直接给出两者约束差异的显式比较陈述。
